nodes.name: Adversarial Network Optimization (ANO)
nodes.statement: Motivated by these two challenges, this paper considers optimizing an abstract utility function associated with the scheduler's action (the so-called utility maximization task \citep{neely2008fairness}) even when the network is non-stationary (which we call Adversarial Network Optimization, or ANO in short) and the feedback model is bandit style.
nodes.statement_short: ANO: utility maximization when the network is non-stationary and feedback is bandit style.

nodes.name: Bandit feedback model
nodes.statement: More formally, if an action $a$ is associated with outcome $O_t(a)$ (for example, arrival and service rates) in round $t$. Then \textit{i)} the scheduler has to decide action $a_t$ without having any information about $O_t(a)$, and \textit{ii)} after playing $a_t$, it can only observe $O_t(a_t)$ but not those $O_t(a')$'s for $a'\neq a$.
nodes.statement_short: Under bandit feedback the scheduler picks $a_t$ blind and then only sees the outcome $O_t(a_t)$ of the chosen action.

nodes.name: Bold-letter vector notation
nodes.statement: We use bold letters to denote vectors, \textit{e.g.}, $\bm q_t,\bm \mu_t,\bm \lambda_t$, and denote their elements with corresponding normal letters, \textit{e.g.}, $q_{t,i},\mu_{t,i},\lambda_{t,i}$.

nodes.name: Integer range [n]
nodes.statement: For an integer $n\ge 0$, $[n]$ stands for $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$.

nodes.name: Probability simplex
nodes.statement: For a finite set $\mathcal S$, $\triangle(\mathcal S)$ is the simplex over $\mathcal S$, \textit{i.e.}, $\{\bm x\in \mathbb R^{\lvert \mathcal S\rvert}\mid \sum_{i=1}^{\lvert \mathcal S\rvert} x_i=1\}$, where every element $\bm x\in \triangle(\mathcal S)$ is a discrete probability distribution over $\mathcal S$.

nodes.name: Big-O and soft-O notation
nodes.statement: We use $\operatorname{\mathcal O}$ to hide all absolute constants, and use $\operatorname{\widetilde{\mathcal O}}$ to additionally hide all logarithmic factors.

nodes.name: Asymptotic notation in T
nodes.statement: For functions $f(T)$ and $g(T)$, we say $f(T)=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(g(T))$ if $\limsup_{T\to \infty} \frac{f(T)}{g(T)}<\infty$ and $f(T)=o_T(g(T))$ if $\limsup_{T\to \infty} \frac{f(T)}{g(T)}=0$.
nodes.statement_short: $f=O_T(g)$ if limsup f/g is finite, and $f=o_T(g)$ if it is zero.

nodes.name: Servers and data links
nodes.statement: Specifically, in a network with multiple servers and directional data links, we denote the set of all servers by ${\mathcal N}$ and that of all data links by ${\mathcal L}\subseteq {\mathcal N}\times {\mathcal N}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Finite network
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\lvert {\mathcal N}\rvert$ and $\lvert {\mathcal L}\rvert$ are both finite.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Commodities
nodes.statement: There are $\lvert {\mathcal N}\rvert$ commodities of jobs such that those jobs belonging to commodity $k\in {\mathcal N}$ are destined for server $k\in {\mathcal N}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Queue Q_n^(k)
nodes.statement: We denote $Q_n^{(k)}$ as the queue of unfinished commodity-$k$ jobs at server $n$, where $n\in {\mathcal N}$ and $k\in {\mathcal N}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation
differentia: of unfinished commodity-$k$ jobs at server $n$

nodes.name: Non-interfering links
nodes.statement: We assume the links do not interfere with each other.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Horizon T
nodes.statement: The scheduling problem lasts for $T>0$ rounds.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Scheduler decisions: arrival rates and link rate allocations
nodes.statement: In round $t\in [T]$, the scheduler makes two decisions: \textit{i)} \textit{arrival rates} of commodity-$k$ jobs into server $n$, $\forall n\in {\mathcal N},k\in {\mathcal N}$, and \textit{ii)} \textit{link rate allocations} of transmitting how many commodity-$k$ jobs over data link $(n,m)$, $\forall k\in {\mathcal N},(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Arrival rate matrix and action set
nodes.statement: In every round $t$, the scheduler decides an $\lvert {\mathcal N}\rvert\times \lvert {\mathcal N}\rvert$ dimensional arrival rate matrix $\bm \lambda(t)$ from some fixed action set $\Lambda\subseteq \mathbb R_{\ge 0}^{\lvert {\mathcal N}\rvert\times \lvert {\mathcal N}\rvert}$, and consequently, $\lambda_n^{(k)}(t)$ jobs with commodity $k$ will be added to queue $Q_n^{(k)}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Utility function g_t
nodes.statement: The arrival rate vector $\bm \lambda(t)$ is associated with some abstract utility $g_{t}(\bm \lambda(t))$ where $g_t\colon \Lambda\to \mathbb R$ is concave (that is, the user's marginal return diminishes gradually as the arrivals increase \citep{huang2011utility,huang2012lifo}), $L$-Lipschitz, and $[-G,G]$-bounded, where $L$ and $G$ here are known constants.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation
nodes.statement_short: Each arrival vector earns utility $g_t(\lambda(t))$, with $g_t$ concave, $L$-Lipschitz and bounded by $G$.

nodes.name: Oblivious adversary model
nodes.statement: Following the adversarial network assumption, we allow $g_t$'s to be time-dependent (though they have to be pre-determined, which is called the \textit{oblivious adversary} model).
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Bandit feedback on utility
nodes.statement: Following the bandit feedback model, the scheduler has no information about $g_t$ before the decision, and can only observe $g_t(\bm \lambda(t))$ for the chosen $\bm \lambda(t)$ but not the whole $g_t$ after decision.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Link capacity C_{n,m}(t)
nodes.statement: We denote the capacity of $(n,m)$ in round $t$ as $C_{n,m}(t)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Bounded capacities
nodes.statement: We assume the capacities are always bounded by some finite constant $M$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Link allocation plan
nodes.statement: Nevertheless, the scheduler can still decide a \textit{link allocation} plan which assigns a distribution over commodities on each link, or formally denoted as $\bm a_{n,m}(t)\in \triangle({\mathcal N})$ (the $|{\mathcal N}|$-dimension distribution simplex, representing the portion of rates allocated to each commodity over the link).
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Stochastic transmissions
nodes.statement: Formally, we assume that after deciding link allocation plans $\{\bm a_{n,m}(t)\in \triangle({\mathcal N})\}_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}$, the number of jobs successfully sent from $Q_n^{(k)}$ to $Q_m^{(k)}$, denoted by $\mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)$, are independently generated such that $\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[\mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)]=C_{n,m}(t) a_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)$ and $\mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)\in [0,M]$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation
nodes.statement_short: Transmitted jobs $\mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)\in[0,M]$ are independent with mean $C_{n,m}(t)a_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)$.

nodes.name: Post-decision observation of capacities
nodes.statement: Again, we assume a bandit fededback model, which means the scheduler is able to observe $C_{n,m}(t)$ and $\bm \mu_{n,m}(t)$ for all $(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}$ only after the decision is made at the end of round $t$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation

nodes.name: Multi-hop queue dynamics
nodes.statement: Putting the two components together, by denoting the length of $Q_n^{(k)}$ at the beginning of round $t$ to be $Q_n^{(k)}(t)$, the network dynamics can then be characterized as follows: \begin{equation} Q_n^{(k)}(t+1)=\begin{cases} \left [Q_n^{(k)}(t)-\sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}\mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)\right ]_+ + \sum_{(o,n)\in {\mathcal L}} \mu_{o,n}^{(k)}(t) + \lambda_{n}^{(k)}(t),&k\ne n\\ 0,&k=n \end{cases}, \end{equation} where $\lambda_n^{(k)}(t)$ is the number of jobs with commodity $k$ that the scheduler adds to server $n$, and $\mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)$ is the number of jobs with commodity $k$ transmitted along data link $(n,m)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation
nodes.statement_short: Each queue loses its outgoing transmissions (clipped at 0) and gains incoming transmissions plus new arrivals; destination queues are 0.

nodes.name: Multi-hop queue dynamics equation
nodes.statement: Q_n^{(k)}(t+1)=\begin{cases} \left [Q_n^{(k)}(t)-\sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}\mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)\right ]_+ + \sum_{(o,n)\in {\mathcal L}} \mu_{o,n}^{(k)}(t) + \lambda_{n}^{(k)}(t),&k\ne n\\ 0,&k=n \end{cases},
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation
nodes.label: eq:multi-hop stability dynamics

nodes.name: Network stability
nodes.statement: However, a scheduling algorithm is meaningless if it cannot ensure network stability, which requires the average number of jobs remaining in the network is non-divergent when the number of rounds is large enough. Formally, the network stability requirement says \begin{equation} \frac 1T \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]=\frac 1T\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_{n}^{(k)}(t)\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(1),\quad \text{when }T\gg 0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation
nodes.statement_short: Network stability: the time-averaged expected total queue length stays $O_T(1)$.

nodes.name: Network stability condition
nodes.statement: \frac 1T \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]=\frac 1T\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_{n}^{(k)}(t)\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(1),\quad \text{when }T\gg 0.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation
nodes.label: eq:average queue

nodes.name: Utility maximization subject to network stability
nodes.statement: The scheduler aims to maximize its average utility subject to the network stability condition, \textit{i.e.}, \begin{equation} \text{Maximize }\frac 1T \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T g_t(\bm \lambda(t))\right ]\text{ s.t. \Cref{eq:average queue} holds}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation
nodes.statement_short: Maximize the average expected utility subject to network stability.

nodes.name: Utility maximization objective
nodes.statement: \text{Maximize }\frac 1T \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T g_t(\bm \lambda(t))\right ]\text{ s.t. \Cref{eq:average queue} holds}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Adversarial Network Optimization under Bandit Feedback Formulation
nodes.label: eq:average reward

nodes.name: Adversarial arrival rates (network stability task)
nodes.statement: To avoid such trivial algorithms, we assume the arrival rates are adversarially chosen for now. That is, $\bm \lambda(t)\in [0,R]^{\lvert {\mathcal N}\rvert\times \lvert {\mathcal N}\rvert}$ is some arbitrary, unknown, and time-varying vector following the oblivious adversary model. It is only revealed post-decision, at the end of round $t$.
nodes.section: 3 Network Stability in Adversarial Multi-Hop Networks
nodes.statement_short: For the stability task, arrival rates in $[0,R]$ are chosen by an oblivious adversary and revealed after decisions.

nodes.name: NSO (Network Stability via Online Linear Optimization)
nodes.statement: \caption{\texttt{NSO}\xspace: \textbf{N}etwork \textbf{S}tability via Online Linear \textbf{O}ptimization} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \REQUIRE{Number of rounds $T$, set of servers ${\mathcal N}$ and links ${\mathcal L}$, maximum capacity $M$, feasible arrival rates $\Lambda$ (adversarial arrival rates given during execution -- only assumed in this section). An online linear optimization algorithm $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace$ (\Cref{alg:OLO unbounded}).} \STATE For each link $(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}$, initialize an instance of $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace$ with action set $\triangle({\mathcal N})$ as $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace_{n,m}$. \FOR{$t=1,2,\ldots,T$} \STATE For each link $(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}$, pass the maximum loss magnitude for this round $M\lVert \bm Q_m(t)-\bm Q_n(t)\rVert_\infty$ to $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace_{n,m}$. Pick link allocation $\bm a_{n,m}(t)\in \triangle({\mathcal N})$ as the output of $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace_{n,m}$. \STATE Observe arrival rates $\bm \lambda(t)\in \Lambda$. \COMMENT{In the utility maximization algorithm \texttt{UMO}\textsuperscript{\texttt{2}}\xspace (\Cref{alg:utility}), this step will be replaced by another algorithmic component.} \STATE Observe capacities $\{C_{n,m}(t)\}_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}$ and actual data transmissions $\{\mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)\}_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L},k\in {\mathcal N}}$. \STATE Calculate queue lengths $\bm Q(t+1)$ from $\bm Q(t)$ according to \Cref{eq:multi-hop stability dynamics}. \STATE For each link $(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}$, pass the loss vector $C_{n,m}(t)(\bm Q_m(t)-\bm Q_n(t))$ to $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace_{n,m}$. \ENDFOR \end{algorithmic}
nodes.section: 3 Network Stability in Adversarial Multi-Hop Networks
input: Number of rounds $T$, set of servers ${\mathcal N}$ and links ${\mathcal L}$, maximum capacity $M$, feasible arrival rates $\Lambda$ (adversarial arrival rates given during execution -- only assumed in this section)
An online linear optimization algorithm $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace$ (\Cref{alg:OLO unbounded})
nodes.statement_short: Run one AdaPFOL instance per link, feeding it queue-differential losses, to choose link allocations that stabilize the network.
nodes.label: alg:stability

nodes.name: Informal Lyapunov drift bound
nodes.statement: &\quad -\frac 12 N^2 ((NM)^2+2(NM)^2+2R^2) T \nonumber\\ &\le \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_{n}^{(k)}(t) \left (\sum_{(o,n)\in {\mathcal L}} \mu_{o,n}^{(k)}(t) + \lambda_n^{(k)}(t) - \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) \right )\right ],
nodes.label: eq:multi-hop stability Lyapunov informal

nodes.name: OLO objective for link scheduling (informal)
nodes.statement: \text{Minimizing }&\quad \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \sum_{k=1}^K \mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) (Q_m^{(k)}(t)-Q_n^{(k)}(t))\right ] \nonumber\\ &=\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \langle \bm Q_m(t)-\bm Q_n(t),\bm \mu_{n,m}(t)\rangle\right ]\nonumber\\ &=\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \langle C_{n,m}(t) (\bm Q_m(t)-\bm Q_n(t)),\bm a_{n,m}(t)\rangle\right ],
nodes.statement_short: Minimizing the drift bound reduces to minimizing a linear loss in the link allocations.
nodes.label: eq:multi-hop stability OLO objective informal

nodes.name: Comparison with single-hop objective of Huang et al.
nodes.statement: While having similarities, this objective is different from that of \citet{huang2023queue} in two aspects: First, the network topology in \citep{huang2023queue} is a single-server, single-hop one, thus it suffices to conduct the Lyapunov drift optimization on the centralized server. In contrast, due to our multi-hop topology, our optimization task \Cref{eq:multi-hop stability OLO objective informal} has to be distributed onto every data link $(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}$ and extra efforts are needed to ensure a good overall scheduling effect. Second, the coefficient $C_{n,m}(t) (Q_m^{(k)}(t)-Q_n^{(k)}(t))$ before $a_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)$ can be either positive or negative, whereas that of \citet{huang2023queue} is always non-negative. Such a negativity also increases the difficulty as many online learning algorithms are typically bad at handling potentially negative losses, see, \textit{e.g.}, \citep{zheng2019equipping,dai2023refined}.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike prior single-hop work, the objective must be distributed over every link and its coefficients may be negative.

nodes.name: Informal self-bounding argument
nodes.statement: &\quad \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]\lesssim \text{Online Learning Performance} \lesssim \operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(T) + o_T(T^{1/4}) \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]^{3/4} \nonumber \\ &\Longrightarrow \frac 1T \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ] = \operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(1),\textit{ i.e.},\text{ the system is stabilized}.
nodes.label: eq:self-bounding informal

nodes.name: Multi-Hop Piecewise Stability for Network Stability
nodes.statement: There exists a reference action sequence $\{\mathring{\bm a}(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$ (where $\mathring{\bm a}(t)=\{\mathring{\bm a}_{n,m}(t)\in \triangle({\mathcal N})\}_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}$, in analogue to the scheduler's action sequence), such that there are some constants $C_W\ge 0$, $\epsilon_W\ge 0$ and a partition $W_1,W_2,\ldots,W_J$ of $[T]$,\footnote{A partition $W_1,W_2,\ldots,W_N$ of $[T]$ is a collection of a few non-intersecting intervals whose union is $[T]$} which ensure that $\sum_{j=1}^J (\lvert W_j\rvert-1)^2\le C_W T$ and \begin{align} &\frac{1}{\lvert W_j\rvert} \sum_{t\in W_j} \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} C_{n,m}(t) \mathring a_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) \ge \epsilon_W + \frac{1}{\lvert W_j\rvert} \sum_{t\in W_j} \left (\lambda_n^{(k)}(t) + \sum_{(o,n)\in {\mathcal L}} C_{o,n}(t) \mathring a_{o,n}^{(k)}(t)\right ), \nonumber\\ &\quad \forall j\in [J],n\in {\mathcal N},k\in {\mathcal N}, \end{align} where $\lambda_n^{(k)}(t)$ is the obliviously decided arrival rates that we assume in this section.
nodes.statement_short: A reference link-allocation sequence and a window partition exist such that, on every window, each queue's average service exceeds its average arrivals by $\epsilon_W$.
nodes.label: def:multi-hop stability network stability

nodes.name: Piecewise stability inequality
nodes.statement: &\frac{1}{\lvert W_j\rvert} \sum_{t\in W_j} \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} C_{n,m}(t) \mathring a_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) \ge \epsilon_W + \frac{1}{\lvert W_j\rvert} \sum_{t\in W_j} \left (\lambda_n^{(k)}(t) + \sum_{(o,n)\in {\mathcal L}} C_{o,n}(t) \mathring a_{o,n}^{(k)}(t)\right ), \nonumber\\ &\quad \forall j\in [J],n\in {\mathcal N},k\in {\mathcal N},
nodes.label: eq:multi-hop stability network stability

nodes.name: Piecewise stability vs. classical capacity region
nodes.statement: Such assumptions are typical in network optimization literature. In the case when the network is stationary, \Cref{def:multi-hop stability network stability} recovers the classical capacity region assumption in SNO \citep{neely2010stochastic}. However, extending this condition to adversarial network is highly non-trivial. For adversarial networks, an alternative assumption is the $(W,\epsilon)$-constrained dynamics assumption \citep{liang2018minimizing}, which roughly says \Cref{eq:multi-hop stability network stability} holds for every window of size $W$. \Cref{def:multi-hop stability network stability} thus allows more flexibility. Finally, our \Cref{def:multi-hop stability network stability} can be viewed as a generalization of the piecewise stability assumption \citep{huang2023queue}, which was crafted for a single centralized server.
nodes.label: remark:assumption

nodes.name: Ability of reference policy in stabilizing the network
nodes.statement: If $\{\mathring{\bm a}(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$ satisfies \Cref{def:multi-hop stability network stability}, then for any scheduler-generated queue lengths $\{\bm Q(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$, \begin{align*} &\quad \epsilon_W \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t)\right ] - (N^2 (2NM+R)^2 + \epsilon_W N^2 (2NM+R)) C_W T \\ &\le-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} C_{n,m}(t) \mathring{a}_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) (Q_m^{(k)}(t) - Q_n^{(k)}(t))\right ]-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t) \lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\right ]. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Under piecewise stability, $\epsilon_W$ times total queue length is bounded by the reference policy's negative drift terms plus $O(C_W T)$.
also_stated_at: If $\{\mathring{\bm a}(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$ satisfies \Cref{def:multi-hop stability network stability}, then for any scheduler-generated queue lengths $\{\bm Q(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$, \begin{align*} &\quad \epsilon_W \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t)\right ] - (N^2 (2NM+R)^2 + \epsilon_W N^2 (2NM+R)) C_W T \\ &\le-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} C_{n,m}(t) \mathring{a}_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) (Q_m^{(k)}(t) - Q_n^{(k)}(t))\right ]-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t) \lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\right ]. \end{align*}
assumptions: $\{\mathring{\bm a}(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$ satisfies \Cref{def:multi-hop stability network stability}
conclusions: for any scheduler-generated queue lengths $\{\bm Q(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$, \begin{align*} &\quad \epsilon_W \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t)\right ] - (N^2 (2NM+R)^2 + \epsilon_W N^2 (2NM+R)) C_W T \\ &\le-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} C_{n,m}(t) \mathring{a}_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) (Q_m^{(k)}(t) - Q_n^{(k)}(t))\right ]-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t) \lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\right ]. \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:multi-hop stability network stability

nodes.name: Lyapunov function and Lyapunov drift
nodes.statement: We carry out our analysis based on the Lyapunov drift analysis \citep[\S 4]{neely2010stochastic}, which considers the Lyapunov function $L_t$ and its drift $\Delta(\bm Q(t))$, defined as follows: \begin{equation*} \text{Lyapunov function }L_t=\frac 12 \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} \left (Q_{n}^{(k)}\right )^2,\quad \text{Lyapunov drift } \Delta(\bm Q(t)) = \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[L_{t+1} - L_t \mid \bm Q(t)]. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Lyapunov Drift Analysis
nodes.statement: Under the queue dynamics of \Cref{eq:multi-hop stability dynamics}, \begin{align} 0\le \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \Delta(\bm Q(t))\right ]&\le \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} \mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)\left (Q_m^{(k)}(t)-Q_n^{(k)}(t)\right ) + \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t) \lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\right ] + \nonumber \\ &\quad \frac 12 N^2 ((NM)^2+2(NM)^2+2R^2) T. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The summed Lyapunov drift is nonnegative and bounded by the transmission/arrival inner products plus $O(N^4M^2+N^2R^2)T$.
also_stated_at: Under the queue dynamics of \Cref{eq:multi-hop stability dynamics}, \begin{align*} 0\le \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \Delta(\bm Q(t))\right ]&\le \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} \mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)\left (Q_m^{(k)}(t)-Q_n^{(k)}(t)\right ) + \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t) \lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\right ] + \nonumber \\ &\quad \frac 12 N^2 ((NM)^2+2(NM)^2+2R^2) T. \end{align*}
assumptions: Under the queue dynamics of \Cref{eq:multi-hop stability dynamics}
conclusions: \begin{align} 0\le \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \Delta(\bm Q(t))\right ]&\le \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} \mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)\left (Q_m^{(k)}(t)-Q_n^{(k)}(t)\right ) + \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t) \lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\right ] + \nonumber \\ &\quad \frac 12 N^2 ((NM)^2+2(NM)^2+2R^2) T. \end{align}
nodes.label: lem:multi-hop stability Lyapunov

nodes.label: eq:multi-hop stability Lyapunov

nodes.name: Per-link OLO objective
nodes.statement: \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \langle \bm \mu_{n,m}(t),\bm Q_m(t)-\bm Q_n(t)\rangle\right ]=\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \langle C_{n,m}(t) (\bm Q_m(t)-\bm Q_n(t)), \bm a_{n,m}(t)\rangle\right ],\quad \forall (n,m)\in {\mathcal L}.
nodes.label: eq:multi-hop OLO objective

nodes.name: Online Linear Optimization
nodes.statement: Consider a $T$-round game. Every round $t\in [T]$, the player selects an action $\bm x_t$ from a convex set $\mathcal X\subseteq \mathbb R^d$. The environment simultaneously decides a loss vector $\bm g_t\in \mathbb R^d$ such that the loss of the player for round $t$ is $\langle \bm x_t,\bm g_t\rangle$. The player will observe the whole vector of $\bm g_t$ (\textit{i.e.}, full-information feedback is available, instead of the more restrictive bandit feedback model). Dynamic regret minimization in OLO considers minimizing \begin{equation*} \text{D-Regret}_T^{\text{OLO}}(\mathring{\bm x}_1,\mathring{\bm x}_2,\ldots,\mathring{\bm x}_T)=\sum_{t=1}^T \langle \bm g_t,\bm x_t-\bm x_t^\circ\rangle,\quad \forall \mathring{\bm x}_1,\mathring{\bm x}_2,\ldots,\mathring{\bm x}_T\in \mathcal X. \end{equation*}
nodes.origin_citation: Zinkevich 2003; McMahan & Streeter 2010; Duchi et al. 2011
nodes.statement_short: OLO: each round the player picks $x_t$ in a convex set, suffers linear loss $\langle x_t,g_t\rangle$, sees $g_t$; dynamic regret against a comparator sequence.
nodes.label: def:OLO

nodes.name: AdaPFOL (Adaptive Parameter-Free Online Learning)
nodes.statement: \caption{\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace: \textbf{Ada}ptive \textbf{P}amameter-\textbf{F}ree \textbf{O}nline \textbf{L}earning} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \REQUIRE{Action set $\mathcal X$. For each round $t$, the maximum loss magnitude $G_t$ will be reveled at the beginning, and a loss vector $\bm g_t$ satisfying $\lVert \bm g_t\rVert_\infty \le G_t$ will be given in the end.} \STATE Set $G\gets 1$. Initialize an instance $\mathcal A$ of the algorithm in \Cref{lem:OLO guarantee} with action set $\mathcal X$. \FOR{$t=1,2,\ldots$} \STATE Observe the maximum loss magnitude $G_t>0$ for this round. \IF{$G_t>G$} \STATE Set $G=2G_t$. Reset $\mathcal A$ as a new instance of the algorithm in \Cref{lem:OLO guarantee} with action set $\mathcal X$. \ENDIF \STATE Output the ouptut of $\mathcal A$. Observe loss vector $\bm g_t$ (such that $\lVert \bm g_t\rVert_\infty\le G_t$). Feed $G^{-1}\bm g_t$ to $\mathcal A$. \ENDFOR \end{algorithmic}
input: For each round $t$, the maximum loss magnitude $G_t$ will be reveled at the beginning, and a loss vector $\bm g_t$ satisfying $\lVert \bm g_t\rVert_\infty \le G_t$ will be given in the end.
nodes.statement_short: Doubling trick over the PFOL algorithm: restart PFOL with scale $2G_t$ whenever the announced loss magnitude exceeds the current scale, feeding it rescaled losses.
nodes.label: alg:OLO unbounded

nodes.name: Guarantee of AdaPFOL Algorithm
nodes.statement: Consider the OLO problem in \Cref{def:OLO}. Let the action set $\mathcal X$ has diameter $D=\sup_{\bm x,\bm y\in \mathcal X}\lVert \bm x-\bm y\rVert_1$. Suppose that $\lVert \bm g_t\rVert_\infty\le G_t$, where $G_t$ is some $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable random variable and $(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T$ is the natural filtration, \textit{i.e.}, $\mathcal F_t$ is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by all random observations made during the first $t$ rounds. Then, \texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace (\Cref{alg:OLO unbounded}) ensures that for any comparator sequence $\mathring{\bm x}_1,\mathring{\bm x}_2,\ldots,\mathring{\bm x}_T\in \mathcal X$, if $\max_{t\in [T]} G_t\ge 1$, then \begin{equation*} \text{D-Regret}_T^{\text{OLO}}(\mathring{\bm x}_1,\mathring{\bm x}_2,\ldots,\mathring{\bm x}_T)=\operatorname{\mathcal O}\left (\sqrt{D \left (D+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \lVert \mathring{\bm x}_t-\mathring{\bm x}_{t+1}\rVert_1\right )}\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm g_t\rVert_\infty^2}\log T \log \left (\max_{t=1}^T G_t\right )\right ). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: AdaPFOL's dynamic regret is $O(\sqrt{D(D+P_T)}\sqrt{\sum_t\|g_t\|_\infty^2}\log T\log\max_t G_t)$ even with unbounded losses.

nodes.name: Path length in dynamic regret
nodes.statement: Note that in general, it is impossible to guarantee $\text{D-Regret}_T^{\text{OLO}}(\mathring{\bm x}_1,\mathring{\bm x}_2,\ldots,\mathring{\bm x}_T)=o_T(T)$ simultaneously for all $\{\mathring{\bm x}_t\in \mathcal X\}_{t\in [T]}$ \citep{zinkevich2003online}. Therefore, many dynamic regret bounds, including ours, depend on the notion of {path length} $P_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \lVert \mathring{\bm x}_t-\mathring{\bm x}_{t+1}\rVert$. Although the path length is linear in $T$ in the worst case, $\text{D-Regret}_T^{\text{OLO}}(\mathring{\bm x}_1,\mathring{\bm x}_2,\ldots,\mathring{\bm x}_T)=o_T(T)$ can still be ensured in cases where $P_T=o_T(T)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sublinear dynamic regret for all comparators is impossible, so bounds depend on the comparator path length $P_T$.
nodes.label: remark:dynamic regret

nodes.name: Deciding a(t) via AdaPFOL Algorithm
nodes.statement: For each link $(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}$, as we did in \texttt{NSO}\xspace, we execute an instance of \texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace (\Cref{alg:OLO unbounded}) where $\mathcal X=\triangle({\mathcal N})$, $\bm g_t=C_{n,m}(t) (\bm Q_m(t) - \bm Q_n(t))$, and $G_t=M\lVert \bm Q_m(t)-\bm Q_n(t)\rVert_\infty$. We make their outputs $\bm x_t$ as $\bm a_{n,m}(t)$ for every round $t$. Let $\mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)$ be the number of actually transmitted jobs from $Q_n^{(k)}(t)$ to $Q_m^{(k)}(t+1)$ induced by $a_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)$. Consider an arbitrary reference action sequence $\{\mathring{\bm a} (t)\}_{t\in [T]}$ satisfying \Cref{def:multi-hop stability network stability}. Let $\mathring{\mu}_{n,m}^{(k)} (t)=C_{n,m}(t) \mathring{a}_{n,m}^{(k)} (t)\in [0,M]$ (as $C_{n,m}(t)\in [0,M]$ and $\mathring a_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)\in [0,1]$). Then \begin{align*} &\quad \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} (\mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)-\mathring{\mu}_{n,m}^{(k)}(t))\left (Q_m^{(k)}(t)-Q_n^{(k)}(t)\right )\right ]\\ &=\operatorname{\mathcal O}\left (M\sqrt{1+P_T^a} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_2^2} \log T \log \left (\max_{t=1}^T \max_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} M \lVert \bm Q_m(t) - \bm Q_n(t)\rVert_\infty\right )\right ]\right )\text{,} \end{align*} where $P_T^a\triangleq \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \lVert \mathring{\bm a}_{n,m}(t) - \mathring{\bm a}_{n,m}(t+1)\rVert_1$ is the path length of $\{\mathring{\bm a}(t)\}_{t=1}^T$.

nodes.name: Main Theorem for Multi-Hop Network Stability
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\{\mathring{\bm a}_{n,m}(t)\in \triangle({\mathcal N})\}_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L},t\in [T]}$ satisfies \Cref{def:multi-hop stability network stability} and its path length satisfies \footnote{This assumption on path lengths comes from \citep[Assumption 2]{huang2023queue}. As discussed in \Cref{remark:dynamic regret}, such conditions are necessary.} \begin{equation} P_t^a\triangleq \sum_{s=1}^{t-1} \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \lVert \mathring{\bm a}_{n,m}(s) - \mathring{\bm a}_{n,m}(s+1)\rVert_1\le C^a t^{1/2 - \delta_a},\quad \forall t=1,2,\ldots,T, \end{equation} where $C^a$ and $\delta_a$ are assumed to be known constants but the precise $P_t^a$ or $\{\mathring{\bm a}_{n,m}(t)\in \triangle({\mathcal N})\}_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L},t\in [T]}$ both remain unknown. Then, if we execute the \texttt{NSO}\xspace framework in \Cref{alg:stability} with \texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace defined in \Cref{alg:OLO unbounded}, the following performance guarantee is enjoyed: \begin{equation*} \frac 1T\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}\left (\frac{(N^2(2NM+R)^2 + \epsilon_W N^2 (2NM+R))C_W + (N^4 M^2 + N^2 R^2)}{\epsilon_W}\right )+o_T(1). \end{equation*} That is, when $T\gg 0$, we have $\frac{1}{T} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(1)$, \textit{i.e.}, \Cref{eq:average queue} holds and the system is stable.

nodes.name: Mildly varying reference policies and comparison with prior work
nodes.statement: Any reference policy $\{\mathring{\bm a}(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$ satisfying \Cref{eq:network stability path length} is called ``mildly varying''. As mentioned in \Cref{remark:dynamic regret}, it is impossible to achieve non-trivial performance without restricting the reference sequence. We also compare our result with two previous results \citep{huang2023queue,yang2023learning} which also ensured network stability in adversarial networks under bandit feedback: Under a path length assumption similar to but looser than \Cref{eq:network stability path length}, \citet{huang2023queue} stabilized single-server networks. By assuming the environment (instead of the reference policy which we do) is mildly varying, \citet{yang2023learning} stabilized single-hop networks. Thus, \Cref{thm:multi-hop stability main theorem} is the first guarantee applicable to adversarial multi-hop networks under bandit feedback.
nodes.section: 3.5 Main Theorem for Multi-Hop Network Stability
nodes.statement_short: Reference policies meeting the path-length condition are called mildly varying; the result is the first stability guarantee for adversarial multi-hop networks under bandit feedback.
nodes.label: remark:stability main theorem

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the multi-hop network stability theorem
nodes.statement: The first step of the proof is comparing the guarantee from \Cref{def:multi-hop stability network stability} and that from Lyapunov drift analysis. Specifically, recall that \Cref{lem:multi-hop stability network stability} upper bounds the total queue length using $-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \langle \bm C_{n,m}(t) (\bm Q_m(t) - \bm Q_n(t)),\mathring{\bm a}_{n,m}(t)\rangle]$ (together with some other terms, which are constants after taking expectations) while \Cref{lem:multi-hop stability Lyapunov} reveals the non-positivity of $-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[\sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \langle \bm C_{n,m}(t) (\bm Q_m(t) - \bm Q_n(t)),{\bm a}_{n,m}(t)\rangle]$ (again, many constants omitted). Furthermore, via the guarantee of \texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace (\Cref{alg:OLO unbounded}) in \Cref{thm:multi-hop stability decision making}, these two terms are actually pretty close -- they only differ by $\operatorname{\widetilde{\mathcal O}}_T\left (\sqrt{1+C^a T^{1/2-\delta_a}} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_2^2}\right ]\right )$, where we used the assumption that $P_T^a\le C^a T^{1/2-\delta_a}$. By a property that ensures $\sum_{t=1}^T x_t^2 \le 4(\sum_{t=1}^T x_t)^{1/5}$ when $\lvert x_t-x_{t+1}\rvert\le 1$ (\Cref{lem:2 upper bound}), this $\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_2^2}\right ]$ can be controlled by $\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]^{3/4}$. Finishing these steps, which are detailed in \Cref{lem:multi-hop stability tedious calc}, we are able to conclude \begin{equation*} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]\le f(T) + g(T) \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]^{3/4} \log \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ], \end{equation*} where $f(T) = \operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(T)$ and $g(T) = \operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(T^{1/4-\delta_a/2})$ are some abstract functions to simplify notations. Therefore, this inequality is in a self-bounding form that $y\le f+y^{3/4} g \log y$ where $y$ is the total queue lengths in $T$ rounds. As we informally stated in \Cref{eq:self-bounding informal}, this gives our system stability guarantee. Indeed, in \Cref{lem:3/4 with log self-bounding}, we show that $y\le f+y^{3/4} g \log y$ implies $y=\operatorname{\mathcal O}(f)+\operatorname{\widetilde{\mathcal O}}(g^4)$. Therefore, $y=\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(T)+\operatorname{\widetilde{\mathcal O}}_T(T^{1-2\delta_a})$ and thus $\frac 1T \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(1)$.
nodes.section: 3.5 Main Theorem for Multi-Hop Network Stability
nodes.statement_short: Combine piecewise stability, Lyapunov drift and the AdaPFOL guarantee into a self-bounding inequality $y\le f+y^{3/4}g\log y$, then solve it.

nodes.name: UMO2 (Utility Maximization via Online Linear Optimization and Bandit Convex Optimization)
nodes.statement: \caption{\texttt{UMO}\textsuperscript{\texttt{2}}\xspace: \textbf{U}tility \textbf{M}aximization via Online Linear \textbf{O}ptimization and Bandit Convex \textbf{O}ptimization} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \REQUIRE{Number of rounds $T$, set of servers ${\mathcal N}$ and links ${\mathcal L}$, maximum capacity $M$, feasible arrival rates $\Lambda$. Parameter $V$. An online linear optimization algorithm $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace$ (\Cref{alg:OLO unbounded}) and a bandit convex optimization algorithm $\texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace$ (\Cref{alg:ABGD}).} \STATE For each link $(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}$, initialize an instance of $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace$ with action set $\triangle({\mathcal N})$ as $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace_{n,m}$. \STATE {\color{blue} Initialize an instance of $\texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace$ with action set $\Lambda$.} \FOR{$t=1,2,\ldots,T$} \STATE For each link $(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}$, pass the maximum loss magnitude for this round $M\lVert \bm Q_m(t)-\bm Q_n(t)\rVert_\infty$ to $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace_{n,m}$. Pick link allocation $\bm a_{n,m}(t)\in \triangle({\mathcal N})$ as the output of $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace_{n,m}$. \STATE {\color{blue}Call $\texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace$ with learning rates defined in \Cref{eq:true learning rate in BCO}. Pick arrival rates $\bm \lambda(t)\in \Lambda$ as its output. \begin{align} \eta_t&=\left (C^\lambda T^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda}\middle / \substack{\left (C^\lambda T^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda}\right )^{7/3} \left (4r^{-3} d^2 \right )^{28/9} \left (M+R\right )^{4/3}+\\ C^\lambda T^{1/2-\delta_\lambda} (r^{-3} d^2 VG^2 / L)^{4/3}+\\ \sum_{s=1}^t \left ((\lVert \bm q_s\rVert_\infty + VG)^2 (\lVert \bm q_s\rVert_2 + VL)^2\right )^{1/3}}\right )^{3/4}, \nonumber\\ \delta_t &= \left (\eta_t d^2 \frac{(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_\infty + VG)^2}{(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_2 + VL)}\right )^{1/3},\quad \alpha_t = \frac{\delta_t}{r}. \end{align}} \STATE Observe capacities $\{C_{n,m}(t)\}_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}$ and actual data transmissions $\{\mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)\}_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L},k\in {\mathcal N}}$. \STATE Calculate queue lengths $\bm Q(t+1)$ from $\bm Q(t)$ according to \Cref{eq:multi-hop stability dynamics}. \STATE For each link $(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}$, pass the loss vector $C_{n,m}(t)(\bm Q_m(t)-\bm Q_n(t))$ to $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace_{n,m}$. \STATE {\color{blue} Observe the collected utility $g_t(\bm \lambda(t))$. Pass the loss $\langle \bm Q(t),\bm \lambda (t)\rangle - V g_t(\bm \lambda(t))$ to $\texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace$.} \ENDFOR \end{algorithmic}
nodes.section: 3.5 Main Theorem for Multi-Hop Network Stability
input: Number of rounds $T$, set of servers ${\mathcal N}$ and links ${\mathcal L}$, maximum capacity $M$, feasible arrival rates $\Lambda$
An online linear optimization algorithm $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace$ (\Cref{alg:OLO unbounded}) and a bandit convex optimization algorithm $\texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace$ (\Cref{alg:ABGD})
nodes.statement_short: NSO plus an AdaBGD instance that picks arrival rates with queue-adaptive learning rates, fed the drift-plus-penalty loss $\langle Q,\lambda\rangle-Vg_t(\lambda)$.
nodes.label: alg:utility

nodes.name: Queue-adaptive learning-rate schedule for AdaBGD
nodes.statement: \eta_t&=\left (C^\lambda T^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda}\middle / \substack{\left (C^\lambda T^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda}\right )^{7/3} \left (4r^{-3} d^2 \right )^{28/9} \left (M+R\right )^{4/3}+\\ C^\lambda T^{1/2-\delta_\lambda} (r^{-3} d^2 VG^2 / L)^{4/3}+\\ \sum_{s=1}^t \left ((\lVert \bm q_s\rVert_\infty + VG)^2 (\lVert \bm q_s\rVert_2 + VL)^2\right )^{1/3}}\right )^{3/4}, \nonumber\\ \delta_t &= \left (\eta_t d^2 \frac{(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_\infty + VG)^2}{(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_2 + VL)}\right )^{1/3},\quad \alpha_t = \frac{\delta_t}{r}.

also_stated_at: \eta_t&=\left (C^\lambda T^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda}\middle / \substack{\left (C^\lambda T^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda}\right )^{7/3} \left (4r^{-3} d^2 \right )^{28/9} \left (M+R\right )^{4/3}+\\ C^\lambda T^{1/2-\delta_\lambda} (r^{-3} d^2 VG^2 / L)^{4/3}+\\ \sum_{s=1}^t \left ((\lVert \bm q_s\rVert_\infty + VG)^2 (\lVert \bm q_s\rVert_2 + VL)^2\right )^{1/3}}\right )^{3/4}, \nonumber\\ \delta_t &= \left (\eta_t d^2 \frac{(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_\infty + VG)^2}{(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_2 + VL)}\right )^{1/3},\quad \alpha_t = \frac{\delta_t}{r},

\eta_t&=\left (C^\lambda T^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda}\middle / \substack{\left (C^\lambda T^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda}\right )^{7/3} \left (4r^{-3} d^2 \right )^{28/9} \left (M+R\right )^{4/3}+\\ C^\lambda T^{1/2-\delta_\lambda} (r^{-3} d^2 VG^2 / L)^{4/3}+\\ \sum_{s=1}^t \left ((\lVert \bm q_s\rVert_\infty + VG)^2 (\lVert \bm q_s\rVert_2 + VL)^2\right )^{1/3}}\right )^{3/4}, \nonumber\\ \delta_t &= \left (\eta_t d^2 \frac{(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_\infty + VG)^2}{(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_2 + VL)}\right )^{1/3},\quad \alpha_t = \frac{\delta_t}{r},
nodes.statement_short: Learning rate $\eta_t$ decays with the cumulative loss magnitudes and Lipschitz constants; $\delta_t$ and $\alpha_t$ follow from $\eta_t$.
nodes.label: eq:true learning rate in BCO

nodes.name: Trade-off parameter V
nodes.statement: In \Cref{lem:multi-hop utility Lyapunov}, we derive \begin{align} &\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \langle C_{n,m}(t) (\bm Q_m(t) - \bm Q_n(t)), \bm a_{n,m}(t)\rangle\right ] + \nonumber\\ &\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \langle \bm Q_n(t),\bm \lambda_n(t)\rangle\right ] - V \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \bigg (g_t(\bm \lambda(t) - g_t(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)))\bigg )\right ]\gtrsim 0, \end{align} where $V$ is a constant that we can arbitrarily pick for analytical purposes.
nodes.statement_short: The informal drift-plus-penalty inequality, with $V$ a free constant trading off stability and utility.

nodes.name: Informal drift-plus-penalty inequality
nodes.statement: &\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \langle C_{n,m}(t) (\bm Q_m(t) - \bm Q_n(t)), \bm a_{n,m}(t)\rangle\right ] + \nonumber\\ &\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \langle \bm Q_n(t),\bm \lambda_n(t)\rangle\right ] - V \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \bigg (g_t(\bm \lambda(t) - g_t(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)))\bigg )\right ]\gtrsim 0,
nodes.label: eq:multi-hop utility Lyapunov informal

nodes.name: BCO objective for arrival rates (informal)
nodes.statement: \text{Minimize }\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \bigg (\langle \bm Q(t),\bm \lambda(t)\rangle-Vg_t(\bm \lambda(t))\bigg )\right ].
nodes.label: eq:multi-hop utility BCO objective informal

nodes.name: Arrival-rate loss function
nodes.statement: As $g_t$ is defined over all possible $\bm \lambda(t)$'s and $\bm \lambda(t)$ can be arbitrarily chosen from the feasible action set $\Lambda$, we regard ``deciding $\bm \lambda(t)$'' as an learning problem with action set $\Lambda$ (instead of making decisions on each link or server separately in \Cref{sec:multi-hop stability OLO}) where the loss of picking $\bm \lambda$ in round $t$ is $ \ell_t(\bm \lambda)\triangleq \langle \bm Q(t),\bm \lambda\rangle - V g_t(\bm \lambda)$.

nodes.name: Convexity of the arrival-rate loss
nodes.statement: This loss function is convex \textit{w.r.t.} $\bm \lambda$ as $\langle \cdot,\cdot \rangle$ is linear and $g_t$ is concave.
assumptions: $\langle \cdot,\cdot \rangle$ is linear and $g_t$ is concave
conclusions: This loss function is convex \textit{w.r.t.} $\bm \lambda$

nodes.name: Multi-Hop Piecewise Stability for Utility Maximization
nodes.statement: There exists a {reference action sequence} $\{(\mathring{\bm a}(t),\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t))\}_{t\in [T]}$ (where $\mathring{\bm a}(t)=\{\mathring{\bm a}_{n,m}(t)\in \triangle({\mathcal N})\}_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}$ and $\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)=\{\mathring{\bm \lambda}_n(t)\in \Lambda_n\}_{n\in {\mathcal N}}$, in analogue to the scheduler's action sequence) such that there are constants $C_W\ge 0$, $\epsilon_W\ge 0$, and a partition $W_1,W_2,\ldots,W_J$ of $[T]$, such that $\sum_{j=1}^J (\lvert W_j\rvert-1)^2\le C_W T$ and \begin{align*} &\frac{1}{\lvert W_j\rvert} \sum_{t\in W_j} \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} C_{n,m}(t) \mathring a_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) \ge \epsilon_W + \frac{1}{\lvert W_j\rvert} \sum_{t\in W_j} \left (\mathring \lambda_n^{(k)}(t) + \sum_{(o,n)\in {\mathcal L}} C_{o,n}(t) \mathring a_{o,n}^{(k)}(t)\right ),\\ &\quad \forall j\in [J],n\in {\mathcal N},k\in {\mathcal N}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: A reference sequence of link allocations and arrival rates exists that is piecewise stable with margin $\epsilon_W$.
nodes.label: def:multi-hop utility network stability

nodes.name: Ability of reference policy (with arrival rates) in stabilizing the network
nodes.statement: If $\{(\mathring{\bm a}(t),\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t))\}_{t\in [T]}$ satisfies \Cref{def:multi-hop utility network stability}, then for any scheduler-generated queue lengths $\{\bm Q(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$, \begin{align} &\quad \epsilon_W \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t)\right ] - (N^2 (2NM+R)^2 + \epsilon_W N^2 (2NM+R)) C_W T \nonumber\\ &\le-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}\sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} \mathring \mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) (Q_m^{(k)}(t) - Q_n^{(k)}(t))\right ] - \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t) \mathring \lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\right ]. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Analogue of Lemma 3.1 with the reference arrival rates $\mathring\lambda(t)$.
also_stated_at: If $\{(\mathring{\bm a}(t),\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t))\}_{t\in [T]}$ satisfies \Cref{def:multi-hop utility network stability}, then for any scheduler-generated queue lengths $\{\bm Q(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$, \begin{align*} &\quad \epsilon_W \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t)\right ] - (N^2 (2NM+R)^2 + \epsilon_W N^2 (2NM+R)) C_W T \nonumber\\ &\le-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}\sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} \mathring \mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) (Q_m^{(k)}(t) - Q_n^{(k)}(t))\right ] - \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t) \mathring \lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\right ]. \end{align*}
assumptions: $\{(\mathring{\bm a}(t),\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t))\}_{t\in [T]}$ satisfies \Cref{def:multi-hop utility network stability}
conclusions: for any scheduler-generated queue lengths $\{\bm Q(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$, \begin{align} &\quad \epsilon_W \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t)\right ] - (N^2 (2NM+R)^2 + \epsilon_W N^2 (2NM+R)) C_W T \nonumber\\ &\le-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}\sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} \mathring \mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) (Q_m^{(k)}(t) - Q_n^{(k)}(t))\right ] - \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t) \mathring \lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\right ]. \end{align}
nodes.label: lem:multi-hop utility network stability

nodes.name: Reference-policy stability inequality (utility task)
nodes.statement: &\quad \epsilon_W \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t)\right ] - (N^2 (2NM+R)^2 + \epsilon_W N^2 (2NM+R)) C_W T \nonumber\\ &\le-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}\sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} \mathring \mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) (Q_m^{(k)}(t) - Q_n^{(k)}(t))\right ] - \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t) \mathring \lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\right ].
nodes.label: eq:multi-hop utility network stability

nodes.name: Drift-plus-penalty function
nodes.statement: In the Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty (DPP) analysis \citep[Theorem 4.2]{neely2010stochastic}, we consider the DPP function $\Delta(\bm Q(t))-V\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[g_t(\bm \lambda(t)) \mid \bm Q(t)]$, where $V$ is arbitrarily determined for our purpose.

nodes.name: Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty inequality
nodes.statement: &\quad -\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} C_{n,m}(t) (Q_m^{(k)}(t)-Q_n^{(k)}(t))a_{n,m}^{(k)}(t)\right ] \nonumber\\ &\quad -\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \sum_{k\in {\mathcal N}} Q_n^{(k)}(t) \lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\right ]+V \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T (g_t(\bm \lambda(t))-g_t(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)))\right ] \nonumber\\ &\le \frac 12 N^2 ((NM)^2+2(NM)^2+2R^2) T+V \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T (g_t(\bm \lambda(t))-g_t(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)))\right ].
nodes.label: eq:multi-hop utility Lyapunov

nodes.name: Two inequalities to be ensured by learning
nodes.statement: &\scalemath{0.95}{-\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}}\langle \mathring {\bm \mu}_{n,m}(t), \bm Q_m(t) - \bm Q_n(t)\rangle\right ]\lesssim -\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \langle \bm \mu_{n,m}(t), \bm Q_m(t)-\bm Q_n(t)\rangle\right ],~ \text{and}} \nonumber\\ &\scalemath{0.95}{- \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \langle \bm Q_n(t), \mathring {\bm \lambda}_n(t)\rangle\right ]\lesssim -\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{n\in {\mathcal N}} \langle \bm Q_n(t), \bm \lambda_n(t)\rangle\right ]+V \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \bigg (g_t(\bm \lambda(t))-g_t(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t))\bigg )\right ].}
nodes.label: eq:multi-hop utility BCO objective

nodes.name: Bandit Convex Optimization
nodes.statement: Consider a $T$-round game. In round $t=1,2,\ldots,T$, the player picks an action $\bm x_t$ from a convex action set $\mathcal X\subseteq \mathbb R^d$, and the environment simultaneously picks an arbitrary convex loss $\ell_t\colon \mathcal X\to \mathbb R$. The player observes and suffers loss $\ell_t(\bm x_t)$. Dynamic regret minimization in BCO considers minimizing \begin{equation*} \text{D-Regret}_T^{\text{BCO}}(\bm u_1,\bm u_2,\ldots,\bm u_T)=\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T (\ell_t(\bm x_t)-\ell_t(\bm u_t))\right ],\quad \forall \bm u_1,\bm u_2,\ldots,\bm u_T\in \mathcal X. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: BCO: the player picks $x_t$, the environment a convex loss $\ell_t$; only $\ell_t(x_t)$ is observed; dynamic regret against a comparator sequence.
nodes.label: def:BCO

nodes.name: AdaBGD (Adaptive Bandit Gradient Descent)
nodes.statement: \caption{\texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace: \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{B}andit \textbf{G}radient \textbf{D}escent} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \REQUIRE{Action set $\mathcal X$ bounded by $[r,R]$ (\textit{i.e.}, $r\mathbb B\subseteq \mathcal X\subseteq R\mathbb B$), hyper-parameters $\eta_1>\eta_2>\cdots>\eta_T$, $\delta_1,\delta_2,\ldots,\delta_T$, and $\alpha_t\triangleq \delta_t / r,\forall t\in [T]$.} \STATE Initialize $\bm y_1=\bm 0$ (an internal variable of the algorithm). \FOR{$t=1,2,\ldots,T$} \STATE Calculate this round's action $\bm x_t\in \mathcal X$, observe loss $\ell_t(x_t)$, and update internal variable $\bm y_{t+1}$: \begin{equation} \bm x_t=\bm y_t+\delta \bm s_t,\quad \bm y_{t+1}=\text{Proj}_{(1-\alpha_t)\mathcal X}\left [\bm y_t-\eta_t \frac{d}{\delta_t} \ell_t(\bm x_t) \bm s_t\right ], \end{equation} where $\bm s_t\in \mathbb R^d$ is a uniformly sampled unit vector used to estimate gradients \citep{flaxman2005online}. \ENDFOR \end{algorithmic}
input: Action set $\mathcal X$ bounded by $[r,R]$ (\textit{i.e.}, $r\mathbb B\subseteq \mathcal X\subseteq R\mathbb B$)
nodes.statement_short: Bandit gradient descent with one-point gradient estimates, projection onto a shrunk set and time-varying learning rates $\eta_t$.
nodes.label: alg:ABGD

nodes.name: AdaBGD update rule
nodes.statement: \bm x_t=\bm y_t+\delta \bm s_t,\quad \bm y_{t+1}=\text{Proj}_{(1-\alpha_t)\mathcal X}\left [\bm y_t-\eta_t \frac{d}{\delta_t} \ell_t(\bm x_t) \bm s_t\right ],
nodes.label: eq:ABGD

nodes.name: Guarantee of AdaBGD Algorithm
nodes.statement: Suppose that $r\mathbb B\subseteq \mathcal X\subseteq R\mathbb B$, the $t$-th loss $\ell_t$ is bounded by $C_t$ and is $L_t$-Lipschitz. Suppose that $\eta_t$ and $\delta_t$ are both $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable (where $(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T$ is the natural filtration), $\eta_1>\eta_2>\cdots>\eta_T$, and $\alpha_t\triangleq \delta_t / r<1$ \textit{a.s.} for all $t\in [T]$. Then for any fixed $\bm u_1,\bm u_2,\ldots,\bm u_T\in \mathcal X$, the \texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace algorithm in \Cref{alg:ABGD} enjoys the following guarantee: \begin{align*} &\quad \text{D-Regret}_T^{\text{BCO}}(\bm u_1,\bm u_2,\ldots,\bm u_T)=\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T (\ell_t(\bm x_t)-\ell_t(\bm u_t))\right ]\\ &\le \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\frac{7R^2}{4\eta_T}+\frac{P_T R}{\eta_T}+\sum_{t=1}^T \left (\frac{\eta_t}{2} \frac{d^2}{\delta_t^2} C_t^2 + 3L_t \delta_t + L_t \alpha_t R\right )\right ], \end{align*} where $P_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\lVert \bm u_t-\bm u_{t+1}\rVert$ is the path length of the comparator sequence $\{\bm u_t\}_{t\in [T]}$.
nodes.statement_short: AdaBGD's dynamic regret is at most $E[7R^2/(4\eta_T)+P_TR/\eta_T+\sum_t(\eta_t d^2C_t^2/(2\delta_t^2)+3L_t\delta_t+L_t\alpha_tR)]$.
also_stated_at: Suppose that $r\mathbb B\subseteq \mathcal X\subseteq R\mathbb B$, the $t$-th loss $\ell_t$ is bounded by $C_t$ and is $L_t$-Lipschitz. Suppose that $\eta_t$ and $\delta_t$ are both $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable (where $(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T$ is the natural filtration), $\eta_1>\eta_2>\cdots>\eta_T$, and $\alpha_t\triangleq \delta_t / r<1$ \textit{a.s.} for all $t\in [T]$. Then for any fixed $\bm u_1,\bm u_2,\ldots,\bm u_T\in \mathcal X$, the \texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace algorithm in \Cref{alg:ABGD} enjoys the following guarantee: \begin{align*} &\quad \text{D-Regret}_T^{\text{BCO}}(\bm u_1,\bm u_2,\ldots,\bm u_T)=\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T (\ell_t(\bm x_t)-\ell_t(\bm u_t))\right ]\\ &\le \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\frac{7R^2}{4\eta_T}+\frac{P_T R}{\eta_T}+\sum_{t=1}^T \left (\frac{\eta_t}{2} \frac{d^2}{\delta_t^2} C_t^2 + 3L_t \delta_t + L_t \alpha_t R\right )\right ], \end{align*} where $P_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\lVert \bm u_t-\bm u_{t+1}\rVert$ is the path length of the comparator sequence $\{\bm u_t\}_{t\in [T]}$.
assumptions: Suppose that $r\mathbb B\subseteq \mathcal X\subseteq R\mathbb B$, the $t$-th loss $\ell_t$ is bounded by $C_t$ and is $L_t$-Lipschitz.

Suppose that $\eta_t$ and $\delta_t$ are both $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable (where $(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T$ is the natural filtration), $\eta_1>\eta_2>\cdots>\eta_T$, and $\alpha_t\triangleq \delta_t / r<1$ \textit{a.s.} for all $t\in [T]$.
conclusions: for any fixed $\bm u_1,\bm u_2,\ldots,\bm u_T\in \mathcal X$, the \texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace algorithm in \Cref{alg:ABGD} enjoys the following guarantee: \begin{align*} &\quad \text{D-Regret}_T^{\text{BCO}}(\bm u_1,\bm u_2,\ldots,\bm u_T)=\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T (\ell_t(\bm x_t)-\ell_t(\bm u_t))\right ]\\ &\le \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\frac{7R^2}{4\eta_T}+\frac{P_T R}{\eta_T}+\sum_{t=1}^T \left (\frac{\eta_t}{2} \frac{d^2}{\delta_t^2} C_t^2 + 3L_t \delta_t + L_t \alpha_t R\right )\right ], \end{align*} where $P_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\lVert \bm u_t-\bm u_{t+1}\rVert$ is the path length of the comparator sequence $\{\bm u_t\}_{t\in [T]}$.
nodes.label: lem:ABGD guarantee

nodes.name: Deciding lambda(t) via AdaBGD Algorithm
nodes.statement: For the reference arrival rates $\{\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$ defined in \Cref{def:multi-hop utility network stability}, suppose that its path length ensures \begin{equation*} P_t^\lambda\triangleq \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \lVert \mathring{\bm \lambda}({t+1}) - \mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)) \rVert_1\le C^\lambda t^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda},\quad \forall t=1,2,\ldots,T, \end{equation*} where, similar to \Cref{thm:multi-hop stability main theorem}, $C^\lambda$ and $\delta_\lambda$ are assumed to be known constants but the precise $P_t^\lambda$ or $\{\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)\}_{t\in [T]}$ both remain unknown. Suppose that the action set $\Lambda$ is bounded by $[r,R]$ (\textit{i.e.}, $r\mathbb B\subseteq \Lambda\subseteq R\mathbb B$). If we execute \texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace (\Cref{alg:ABGD}) over $\Lambda$ with loss functions $\ell_t(\bm \lambda)=\langle \bm Q(t),\bm \lambda\rangle-V g_t(\bm \lambda)$ and parameters $\eta_t,\delta_t,\alpha_t$ defined in \Cref{eq:true learning rate in BCO} (restated below as \Cref{eq:true learning rate in BCO restatement} to ease reading): \begin{align} \eta_t&=\left (C^\lambda T^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda}\middle / \substack{\left (C^\lambda T^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda}\right )^{7/3} \left (4r^{-3} d^2 \right )^{28/9} \left (M+R\right )^{4/3}+\\ C^\lambda T^{1/2-\delta_\lambda} (r^{-3} d^2 VG^2 / L)^{4/3}+\\ \sum_{s=1}^t \left ((\lVert \bm q_s\rVert_\infty + VG)^2 (\lVert \bm q_s\rVert_2 + VL)^2\right )^{1/3}}\right )^{3/4}, \nonumber\\ \delta_t &= \left (\eta_t d^2 \frac{(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_\infty + VG)^2}{(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_2 + VL)}\right )^{1/3},\quad \alpha_t = \frac{\delta_t}{r}, \end{align} then the outputs $\bm \lambda(1),\bm \lambda(2),\ldots,\bm \lambda(T) \in \Lambda$ of \texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace ensure \begin{align*} &\scalemath{0.95}{\quad \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \left ((\langle \bm Q(t),\bm \lambda(t)\rangle - Vg_t(\bm \lambda(t))) - (\langle \bm Q(t),\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)\rangle - Vg_t(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)))\right )\right ]}\\ &\scalemath{0.95}{=\operatorname{\mathcal O}\left (\frac{R(2NM+R)}{r^7} d^{14/3} (C^\lambda T^{1/2-\delta_\lambda})^2\right )+\operatorname{\mathcal O}\left (\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\left (\frac{R}{r} d^{2/3}+R\right ) (C^\lambda T^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda})^{1/4} \left (\sum_{t=1}^T \left (\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_2 + V(L+G)\right )^{4/3}\right )^{3/4}\right ]\right ).} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: With the queue-adaptive schedule, AdaBGD's arrival rates achieve drift-plus-penalty loss within a queue-dependent $O(T^{1/8-\delta_\lambda/4}(\cdot)^{3/4})$-type term of any mildly varying reference.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of deciding lambda(t) via AdaBGD
nodes.statement: The terms $(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_\infty+VG)$ and $(\lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_2+VL)$ are the boundedness and Lipschitzness of $\ell_t$, respectively, which we denote by $C_t$ and $L_t$ to simplify notations. First suppose that all conditions in \Cref{lem:ABGD guarantee} are satisfied by our $\{\eta_t\}_{t\in [T]}$. To balance the term inside $\sum_{t=1}^T (\cdot)$ in \Cref{lem:ABGD guarantee} by fixing $\eta_t$ and altering $\delta_t$, one shall pick $\delta_t=(\eta_t d^2 C_t^2 / L_t)^{1/3}$ and roughly have (hiding many constant terms; see \Cref{eq:BCO regret decomposition} in the appendix for an accurate form): \begin{equation} \text{D-Regret}_T^{\text{BCO}}(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(1),\mathring{\bm \lambda}(2),\ldots,\mathring{\bm \lambda}(T))\lesssim \frac{C^\lambda T^{1/2-\delta_\lambda}}{\eta_T} + \sum_{t=1}^T \left (\eta_t C_t^2 L_t^2\right )^{1/3}. \end{equation} We derive in \Cref{lem:3/4 summation lemma} that $\sum_{t=1}^T \frac{x_t}{(\sum_{s\le t} x_s)^{1/4}}\lesssim (\sum_{t=1}^T x_t)^{3/4}$, which is a variant of the famous summation lemma \citep{auer2002nonstochastic}. Therefore, if we pick $\eta_t\approx \left (\frac{C^\lambda T^{1/2-\delta_\lambda}}{\sum_{s=1}^t (C_t^2 L_t^2)^{1/3}}\right )^{3/4}$ (\textit{i.e.}, only keeping the third term in the denominator of \Cref{eq:true learning rate in BCO restatement}), \Cref{eq:BCO regret decomposition informal} becomes $\operatorname{\mathcal O}((C^\lambda T^{1/2-\delta_\lambda})^{1/4} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[(\sum_{t=1}^T (C_t^2 L_t^2)^{1/3})^{3/4}])$. When focusing on $T$-related terms, this is roughly $\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(T^{1/8-\delta_\lambda/4} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[(\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1)]^{7/8})$, which allows the self-bounding analysis similar to \Cref{eq:self-bounding informal}. However, such a configuration of $\{\eta_t\}_{t\in [T]}$ may not ensure the $\alpha_t = \delta_t / r = (\eta_t d^2 C_t^2 / L_t)^{1/3}/r<1$ condition in \Cref{lem:ABGD guarantee}. The other two terms in \Cref{eq:true learning rate in BCO restatement} are added for this purpose. We refer the readers to \Cref{sec:general bandit part appendix} for detailed verification.
nodes.statement_short: Balance $\delta_t$ against $\eta_t$ in the AdaBGD bound, then use the 3/4-power summation lemma to choose $\eta_t$; extra denominator terms ensure $\alpha_t<1$.

nodes.name: Informal BCO regret decomposition
nodes.statement: \text{D-Regret}_T^{\text{BCO}}(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(1),\mathring{\bm \lambda}(2),\ldots,\mathring{\bm \lambda}(T))\lesssim \frac{C^\lambda T^{1/2-\delta_\lambda}}{\eta_T} + \sum_{t=1}^T \left (\eta_t C_t^2 L_t^2\right )^{1/3}.
nodes.label: eq:BCO regret decomposition informal

nodes.name: Main Theorem for Multi-Hop Utility Maximization
nodes.statement: Suppose that the feasible set of arrival rates vector $\Lambda$ is bounded by $[r,R]$. Assume all (unknown) utility functions $g_t$ to be concave, $L$-Lipschitz, and $[-G,G]$-bounded. Consider a reference action sequence $\{(\mathring{\bm a}(t),\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t))\}_{t\in [T]}$ satisfying \Cref{def:multi-hop utility network stability}, such that their path lengths satisfy \begin{align*} P_t^a\triangleq \sum_{s=1}^{t-1} \lVert \mathring{\bm a}(s)-\mathring{\bm a}(s+1)\rVert_1\le C^a t^{1/2-\delta_a},~P_t^\lambda\triangleq \sum_{s=1}^{t-1} \lVert \mathring{\bm \lambda}(s)-\mathring{\bm \lambda}(s+1)\rVert_1\le C^\lambda t^{1/2 - \delta_\lambda},\quad \forall t\in [T]. \end{align*} Here, $M,R,r,L,G,C^a,\delta_a,C^\lambda,\delta_\lambda$ are assumed to be known constants, whereas the specific $\{(\mathring{\bm a}(t),\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t))\}_{t\in [T]}$ remains unknown. If we execute the \texttt{UMO}\textsuperscript{\texttt{2}}\xspace framework in \Cref{alg:utility} with the $\texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace$ sub-rountine given in \Cref{alg:OLO unbounded} and the $\texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace$ sub-routine given in \Cref{alg:ABGD}, when $T$ is large enough such that the constant $V=o_T(\min\{T^{2\delta_a/3},T^{2\delta_\lambda/7}\})$, the following inequalities hold simultaneously: \begin{align*} &\scalemath{0.95}{\frac 1T \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}\left (\frac{(N^2 (2NM+R)^2 + \epsilon_W N^2 (2NM+R)) C_W + (N^4 M^2+N^2 R^2)}{\epsilon_W}\right ) + o_T(1),}\\ &\scalemath{0.95}{\frac 1T \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \left (g_{t}(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)) - g_{t}(\bm \lambda(t))\right )\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}\left (\frac{(N^2 (2NM+R)^2 + \epsilon_W N^2 (2NM+R)) C_W + (N^4 M^2+N^2 R^2)}{V}\right ) + o_T(V^{-1}).} \end{align*} That is, when $T\gg 0$, our algorithm not only stabilizes the system so that $\frac 1T \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(1)$, but also enjoys an average utility approaching that of the reference policy polynomially fast, \textit{i.e.}, $\frac 1T \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \left (g_{t}(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)) - g_{t}(\bm \lambda(t))\right )\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(V^{-1})$ -- the utility maximization objective \Cref{eq:average reward} is ensured.

nodes.name: On the condition on V
nodes.statement: The condition $V=o_T(\min\{T^{2\delta_a/3},T^{2\delta_\lambda/7}\})$ says $T$ cannot be too small compared to $V$, which was not an issue in SNO as people often let $T$ approach infinity \citep{neely2008fairness}. Albeit this condition looks restrictive, we remark that $V$ can still be as large as a polynomial of $T$ and thus $\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(V^{-1})$ means a polynomially decaying gap between our utility and that of any mildly varying policies whose path lengths are small -- which is the first guarantee that applies to utility maximization tasks in adversarial networks under bandit feedback. Similar to the discussions in \Cref{remark:stability main theorem}, due to non-stationary environments and bandit feedback, it is highly non-trivial to define ``optimal reference policy'' in ANO. Nevertheless, our mildly varying reference policy class allows optimal policies for SNO settings.
nodes.section: 4.5 Main Theorem for Multi-Hop Utility Maximization
nodes.statement_short: $V$ may still be polynomial in $T$, so the utility gap decays polynomially; first such guarantee for adversarial networks under bandit feedback.
nodes.label: remark:utility main theorem

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the multi-hop utility maximization theorem
nodes.statement: The first step of the proof is plugging the algorithmic guarantees for \texttt{AdaPFOL}\xspace (\Cref{thm:multi-hop stability decision making}) and for \texttt{AdaBGD}\xspace (\Cref{thm:multi-hop utility decision making}) into the reference policy assumption (\Cref{eq:multi-hop utility network stability}) and then making use of the Lyapunov DPP guarantee (\Cref{eq:multi-hop utility Lyapunov}). We present the detailed derivation in \Cref{lem:multi-hop utility tedious calc}. The conclusion reads \begin{align} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]&\le -\frac{V}{\epsilon_W} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \bigg (g_t(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)) - g_t(\bm \lambda(t))\bigg )\right ] + f(T) + \nonumber\\ &\quad g(T) \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]^{3/4} \log \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}} \left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ] + h(T) \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}} \left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]^{7/8}, \end{align} where $f(T)=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(T)$, $g(T)=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(T^{1/4-\delta_a/2})$, and $h(T)=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(T^{1/8-\delta_\lambda/4})$. \paragraph{Step 1 (Develop a Coarse Average Queue Length Bound).} By the boundedness of $g_t$, the first term on the RHS of \Cref{eq:multi-hop utility self-bounding informal} is controlled by $\frac{V}{\epsilon_W} T G=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(VT)$ (note that, as $V=\text{poly}(T)$, $V$ is not a constant that can be hidden in $\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T$ and this term is actually super-linear). Similar to the one used when proving \Cref{thm:multi-hop stability main theorem}, we develop another self-bounding property that says $y\le f+y^{3/4}g\log y +y^{7/8}h$ infers $y=\operatorname{\mathcal O}(f)+\operatorname{\widetilde{\mathcal O}}(g^{4}) + \operatorname{\mathcal O}(h^8)$ (see \Cref{lem:3/4 and 7/8 self-bounding}). Therefore, \begin{equation*} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T\left (VT + T\right ) + \operatorname{\widetilde{\mathcal O}}_T\left (T^{1-2\delta_a}\right ) + \operatorname{\mathcal O}_T\left (T^{1 - 2 \delta_\lambda}\right )=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(VT), \end{equation*} only giving a $\frac 1T\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(V)=\omega_T(1)$ bound on the average queue length (violating the system stability condition \Cref{eq:average queue}). However, this inequality can be used to derive the polynomial convergence result on the utility, which in turn further refines the queue length bound. \paragraph{Step 2 (Yield Polynomial Convergence on the Utility).} Moving the difference in the average utility to the LHS in \Cref{eq:multi-hop utility self-bounding informal} and plugging in the just-derived bound on average queue length, we have \begin{align*} \frac{V}{\epsilon_W T} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \left (g_t(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)) - g_t(\bm \lambda(t)))\right )\right ]&=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T\left (-0+\frac{f(T)}{T}+\frac{g(T)}{T}(VT)^{3/4}+\frac{h(T)}{T}(VT)^{7/8}\right )\\ &=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T\left (1+\left (\frac{T^{1-2\delta_a}V^3}{T}\right )^{1/4}+\left (\frac{T^{1-2\delta_\lambda}V^7}{T}\right )^{1/8}\right ). \end{align*} According to the assumption that $V=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(\min\{T^{2\delta_a/3},T^{2\delta_\lambda/7}\})$, the RHS is of order $\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(1)$. Thus \begin{equation*} \frac 1T \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \left (g_t(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)) - g_t(\bm \lambda(t)))\right )\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(V^{-1}), \end{equation*} \textit{i.e.}, a polynomial convergence rate on the expected average utility is derived. \paragraph{Step 3 (Refine the Average Queue Length Bound).} Now we are ready to refine our average queue length bound. Instead of controlling the utility with boundedness $g_t\in [-G,G]$, we utilize the just-derived convergence result and yields (again using the self-bounding property in \Cref{lem:3/4 and 7/8 self-bounding}) \begin{equation*} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T\left (V \times V^{-1} T + T\right ) + \operatorname{\widetilde{\mathcal O}}_T\left (T^{1-2\delta_a}\right ) + \operatorname{\mathcal O}_T\left (T^{1-2\delta_\lambda}\right )=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(T), \end{equation*} that is, the average queue length $\frac 1T\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]=\operatorname{\mathcal O}_T(1)$, which means \Cref{eq:average queue} holds and the system is stable. Putting Step 2 and Step 3 together gives our conclusion. Once again, we omitted all factors except for those $\text{poly}(T)$ ones throughout this proof sketch. Please refer to \Cref{sec:multi-hop utility appendix} for the complete version.
nodes.section: 4.5 Main Theorem for Multi-Hop Utility Maximization
nodes.statement_short: Derive a self-bounding inequality with utility gap, $y^{3/4}$ and $y^{7/8}$ terms; coarse queue bound, then utility convergence, then refined queue bound.

nodes.statement: \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]&\le -\frac{V}{\epsilon_W} \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \bigg (g_t(\mathring{\bm \lambda}(t)) - g_t(\bm \lambda(t))\bigg )\right ] + f(T) + \nonumber\\ &\quad g(T) \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}\left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]^{3/4} \log \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}} \left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ] + h(T) \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}} \left [\sum_{t=1}^T \lVert \bm Q(t)\rVert_1\right ]^{7/8},

nodes.name: Queue Length Increment
nodes.statement: For every $n\in {\mathcal N}$, $k\in {\mathcal N}$, and $t\in [T]$, we have \begin{equation*} \lvert Q_n^{(k)}(t+1)-Q_n^{(k)}(t)\rvert\le (2NM+R). \end{equation*}
nodes.section: B Omitted Proofs for Multi-Hop Network Stability Tasks
assumptions: For every $n\in {\mathcal N}$, $k\in {\mathcal N}$, and $t\in [T]$
nodes.statement_short: A single queue changes by at most $2NM+R$ per round.
conclusions: \begin{equation*} \lvert Q_n^{(k)}(t+1)-Q_n^{(k)}(t)\rvert\le (2NM+R). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Proof of queue length increment
nodes.statement: According to the queue length dynamics in \Cref{eq:multi-hop stability dynamics}, we know \begin{equation*} \lvert Q_n^{(k)}(t+1)-Q_n^{(k)}(t)\rvert\le \left \lvert \sum_{(n,m)\in {\mathcal L}} \mu_{n,m}^{(k)}(t) + \sum_{(o,n)\in {\mathcal L}} \mu_{o,n}^{(k)}(t) + \lambda_n^{(k)}(t) \right \rvert\le (2NM+R), \end{equation*} which utilizes the assumption that $\lambda_n^{(k)}(t)\in [0,R]$ and $\mu_{(n,m)}^{(k)}(t)\in [0,M]$.
